reels.caption:
Most men aren't lonely in the way headlines describe. They're fine. They have colleagues and a group chat.

The better question is who would know if you weren't.

Who's on your list?

Evidence: Survey Center on American Life (Cox, 2021). Reflection: Moodius. Full essay "The Loneliness of Being Fine" on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: No names needed: how many people are on your list?

reels.hook_b: The maths of friendship nobody told you.
cards: That's an evening a week, for a year.
School scheduled it for you. Adult life doesn't.
So put it in the calendar. Same night, every other week.

source.author: Jeffrey Hall
source.work: How many hours does it take to make a friend? (JSPR 36(4))

reels.caption:
Jeffrey Hall's research estimated roughly 50 hours to go from acquaintance to casual friend, 90 to friend, and more than 200 to close friend.

Nothing in adult life schedules those hours for you. That's the problem, and the fix.

Who would you give the next 200 to?

Evidence: Hall (2019). Aristotle said the same with salt (Nicomachean Ethics VIII.3). Full essay on the Substack, link in bio.
reels.first_comment: Who's one person you'd want to spend the 200 hours with?

notes: A better question than "are you lonely?": if you weren't okay, who would know? Not who would care. Who would notice before you said anything. For many men the list is short, and they'd still say they're fine.

Jeffrey Hall's research estimated around 200 hours together to go from friend to close friend. That's an evening a week for a year. School scheduled those hours. Adult life doesn't. That's most of the male loneliness story, and the fix.

A 2017 meta-analysis of 78 samples found that of all masculine norms, self-reliance was among the few consistently linked to poorer mental health. It doesn't look like a vice. It looks like competence. That's why it's hard to see.
